what_it_does: Hardware designers write chip blueprints in a language called RTL (Register-Transfer Level) — essentially a precise description of how data moves between registers (tiny on-chip memory slots) every clock tick. Writing correct RTL by hand is slow and error-prone, so researchers have tried using large language models (LLMs — AI text generators) to do it automatically. The problem is that a single LLM often produces code with syntax errors or logic bugs, because it must simultaneously manage the hardware description language, a testbench language, and the reasoning needed to verify and fix its own output. MAGE breaks this into a team of specialized AI agents, each with a focused role. One agent generates many diverse candidate RTL snippets by sampling from the LLM at high "temperature" (a setting that produces more varied, exploratory outputs). A second agent inserts checkpoints mid-generation to catch functional errors early and feed precise, targeted correction hints back to the generator. A third agent iteratively debugs the remaining issues. Together the agents are claimed to outperform single-LLM approaches on standard RTL generation benchmarks, though the full paper is needed for a complete picture of the results.
